description: Enforce credential lifecycle limits through automated rotation of passwords, API keys, service account tokens, and secrets. Two distinct tiers of effectiveness: (1) OS-level password aging (chage on Linux, Group Policy on Windows) forces periodic password changes, typically every 90 days — this limits the maximum validity window of compromised credentials but provides minimal protection against immediate credential abuse since attackers typically exploit stolen credentials within hours. NIST SP 800-63B recommends against mandatory periodic rotation for human users due to the pattern of progressively weaker passwords (Password1!, Password2!). (2) Automated short-lived secret rotation via secrets managers (HashiCorp Vault dynamic secrets, AWS STS temporary credentials, Kubernetes service account token projection) with TTLs measured in hours — this genuinely limits the exploitation window because credentials may expire before an attacker can extract and replay them. The attenuation strength is directly proportional to the rotation frequency: 1-hour TTLs provide strong protection, 90-day aging provides weak protection.

cvss_vector_impacts.rationale: Effectiveness is proportional to rotation frequency. For automated short-lived secrets (Vault dynamic secrets with 1-hour TTL, STS temporary credentials), the credential may expire before an attacker can extract and replay it — requiring the attacker to maintain persistent access to the credential source rather than using a one-time theft. For 90-day password aging, the protection window is too large to prevent most credential abuse (attackers act within hours), providing only residual protection against very slow-developing compromises such as leaked credential databases discovered months after breach

verification.method: Verify credential rotation enforcement via password aging (OS-level) and secret TTL policies (application-level)
